assessments.technical_explanation: The flagged pattern-match expression resolves dotted report paths against a ledger object inside a standalone golden-output evaluation script. Examining the expression itself, it consists of a literal prefix, one negated character class, and a single greedy wildcard segment; there are no nested quantifiers or interleaved alternations that could produce exponential backtracking, so the scanner heuristic does not correspond to a real catastrophic-backtracking condition. The matched input originates from the project's own committed fixture rules rather than attacker-controlled data, and the file executes only as a local command-line evaluation harness, not in the SillyTavern extension runtime.
assessments.layman_explanation: An automated scanner thought a text-matching rule in the project's own test tool might hang on crafted input. The rule is actually simple and finishes quickly, it only ever processes the project's own test data, and this tool runs only when a developer runs it locally, not when the extension is used.

assessments.technical_explanation: The expression may permit a local CPU slowdown, but this evidence shows no credential, persistence, code-execution, or cross-user impact.
assessments.layman_explanation: A crafted input might briefly slow or freeze the local client, without showing broader security harm.
assessments.developer_action: Bound the input length or replace the expression when practical.

assessments.technical_explanation: The flagged dynamic function construction appears in a Node-based behavior test harness, not in the script the extension manifest loads at runtime. The test reads the extension's committed entry script from disk, slices out pure widget size and position clamping helpers, compiles them into isolated testable units, and invokes them with synthetic viewport dimensions. The only content ever compiled is the project's own already-executable source; no chat text, network data, saved configuration, or other untrusted input reaches the constructor. An adversary able to alter that committed source would already possess arbitrary code execution in the project, so this construction introduces no new execution path, destination, or persistence.

observations.title: All five dynamic-execution matches are one test-harness extraction pattern over first-party source
observations.technical_explanation: All five candidates sit inside a single behavior test case. The test reads the extension's own entry script from the repository, slices out several named pure helper functions covering display-mode normalization, dimension clamping, settings migration, latest-entry lookup, and widget layout, then constructs functions at runtime from those excerpts with stubbed dependencies so their logic can be asserted in isolation under Node. The evaluated text originates exclusively from the project's own committed source; no chat content, model output, network data, user input, or credentials flow into it, and there is no network access, persistence, or obfuscation. The extension manifest declares only the main entry script for loading, so this test file does not execute in the SillyTavern runtime. The scanner flags the runtime code-construction mechanism, which here is a deliberate and contained testing technique rather than a demonstrated exposure.
observations.layman_explanation: All five flags point at the same thing: a self-test that lifts small pieces of the project's own code and runs them with fake values to check they work. Nothing from users, chats, or the internet is ever executed, so this is not a danger.
observations.developer_action: Review the cited evidence and confirm the intended behavior.
